procedural_history.originating_court: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Bench No. 1, New Delhi
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 8.7.2016 passed by the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission in Consumer Complaint No. 51 of 2006, and the final order dated 11.09.2017.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: There is no High Court proceeding mentioned in the text.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, Mercedes Benz, initially challenged the order dated 08.07.2016 before the Supreme Court by way of filing C.A. No.10410/2016. The Supreme Court disposed of that appeal, directing the National Commission to adjudicate the dispute finally, leaving it open for Mercedes Benz to challenge the order on maintainability as well as the final order. After the final order was passed, Mercedes Benz challenged both the order dated 08.07.2016 and the final order dated 11.09.2017 by way of Civil Appeal Nos. 19536-19537 of 2017 and Civil Appeal No. 2633 of 2018. The respondent-complainant filed a cross-appeal against the order dated 11.09.2017 (Civil Appeal No. 353 of 2008).

decision.appeal_result: C.A. No. 353/2008 partly allowed. C.A. No. 19536 and 19537/2017 and C.A. No. 2633/2018 dismissed. There shall be no order as to costs.

issue.issue_text: whether the purchase of a vehicle/good by a Company for...

facts: A company purchased a high-priced, luxurious car.
The company (the complainant) asserted that the car was purchased for the personal use of its Director and his family as a perquisite.
The seller (the appellant) argued that any purchase by a company is for a 'commercial purpose' and therefore the company is not a 'consumer' under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986.
law: To be considered a 'commercial purpose' under Section 2(1)(d) of the Consumer Protection Act, the purchase of a good or service must have a 'close and direct nexus with a profit-generating activity'.
The onus is on the seller to prove that a good was purchased for a 'commercial purpose'. The buyer does not have to prove it was not.

The Court distinguished between two scenarios: a) A purchase by a company for the personal use of its directors/employees is NOT a commercial purpose. b) A purchase by a company for its own purposes (e.g., profit generation) IS a commercial purpose, even if incidentally used by employees for personal reasons.
application: The Court found that the seller failed to provide any evidence or material to show that the car was used for any commercial purpose or was linked to any profit-generating activity of the company.
The complainant company, however, had specifically stated that the dominant purpose of the purchase was for the personal use of its Director.
The Court reasoned that even if the company claimed an income tax deduction for the car, this was not sufficient to prove a commercial purpose without evidence of a direct link to profit generation.
Because the seller did not meet its burden of proof to show a nexus to a profit-generating activity, the Court concluded the purchase was not for a commercial purpose.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the purchase of a vehicle by a company for the personal use of its director does not amount to a 'commercial purpose' if the seller fails to prove that the purchase has a close and direct nexus with a profit-generating activity of the company. In this case, since no such link was established, the company was deemed a 'consumer' and its complaint was maintainable.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The legal determination of whether a company qualifies as a 'consumer' hinges on the question of whether the purchase of a vehicle or good by the company for the commercial use of its director or employee is excluded from the statutory definition.
obiter: The National Commission should adjudicate the dispute finally and thereafter it will be open to the appellant to challenge the order of maintainability, i.e., the present order as well as the final order.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the purchase of a car by a company for its director's use does not automatically qualify as a 'commercial purpose' unless the appellant can prove its dominant use is linked to profit-generating activity. While upholding the National Commission's finding that the car was defective and the complaint was maintainable, the court modified the relief granted. It reduced the compensation from a full refund (Rs. 58 lakhs) to a partial refund (Rs. 36 lakhs) and allowed the complainant to keep the car, reasoning that it would be inequitable to order a full refund when the complainant had used the vehicle for seventeen years.
legal_tests_applied: To determine if a transaction is for a 'commercial purpose', the court assesses whether the dominant purpose or use of the good is for a commercial purpose or has a nexus to a profit-generating activity of the company; a straitjacket formula cannot be adopted and it depends on the facts and circumstances of each case.
A 'defect' under Section 2(1)(f) of the Consumer Protection Act is a fault, imperfection, or shortcoming in the quality or standard which is expected to be maintained under the contract.
Withholding material information that a seller possesses, such as the trigger level for airbags, constitutes an 'unfair and deceptive trade practice'.
why_appellant_lost: The appellants failed to bring on record any material to show that the dominant purpose or dominant use of the car in question was for commercial purpose or that the purchase of the car had any nexus or was linked with any profit generating activity of the respondent no. 1 company.

The court affirmed the finding that the persistent and excessive overheating of the car, despite rectification measures, constituted an inherent 'defect' as it was a shortcoming in the quality and standard expected of such a vehicle.

The court found that the appellants indulged in an unfair trade practice by withholding material information about the trigger level for the frontal airbags, which they alone knew and ought to have disclosed.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully established that the complaint was maintainable because the car purchased by the company for its director was not used for any activity directly connected with the commercial purpose of earning profit.
The respondent proved that the car suffered from an inherent defect of overheating which caused great inconvenience and discomfort, meeting the legal definition of a 'defect'.

The respondent's victory was partial because the final relief was reduced. The court reasoned that the 'interest of justice and balance of equity' required a modification of the award due to the 'subsequent event of the respondent-complainant having retained and used the car in question for about seventeen years'.
policy_considerations: People do not purchase the high-end luxurious cars to suffer discomfort more particularly when they buy the vehicle keeping utmost faith in the supplier who would make the representations in the brochures or the advertisements projecting and promoting such cars as the finest and safest automobile in the world.
The remedy awarded must consider the principles of justice and equity, which includes accounting for the consumer's prolonged use of the defective product when determining the final compensation.

Sellers and manufacturers have a duty to disclose material information that they exclusively possess to the consumer, and withholding such information constitutes an unfair trade practice intended to promote a sale.
